Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Maria Cowper to Penelope Maitland 7 September 1769 Bodleian Library, University of Oxford MS. Eng. lett. d. 288, fols 55–60 [f.55r] Park1 Sep[tember]. 7. 1769. My most dear sister, Accept my tenderest acknowledgements for your constant enquiries, kind letter, and anxious solicitude for me! unworthy so much precious friendship, as on all sides flows to com - =fort me under my present humbling circumstances2 I, who am ever upon the muse, and too often in deep, melancholy cogitation, looking into each of our Familys at this period of time , per- =ceive such aweful Providences attending us , as call aloud for humiliation and submission!! To trace no further back than June last, my dangerous illness ! Your own dear childs fa - =ding health - poor Theas3 sickness, as soon as they were settl'd at Bingfeild purposing to be happy - Ashley's4 relapse into his old unhappy disorder - dear Martin's5 Loss - my inexpressible 1 Park House, Hertford, Hertfordshire. 2 The circumstances referred to are the death of her husband. William Cowper (1731 –1800) wrote to Maria to offer his condolences on 31 August 1769 (Hertfordshire Archives and Local Studies, DZ/117/1/19, ‘Letter from William Cowper to Maria Cowper of Hertingfordbury Park’, 31 August 1769). 3 Possibly Theodora Jane Cowper, the daughter of Ashley Cowper (d. 1788, Maria’s brother -in-law) and Pennington Goodeve, with who m the poet William Cowper (1731 –1800) fell in love but was prevented from marrying. 4 Ashley Cowper (d. 1788), the brother of Maria ’s husband William Cowper (1722 –1769). 5 Martin Madan (1726 –1790), barrister, clergyman, and writer known for his contributions to Methodist music. He was the brother of Maria and Penelope. His son, William, died in 1769 and so Maria’s reference to his loss presumably refers to the death of his son. Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Zoe Screti; edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 woes - our belov'd mothers accumulated tryals ! and sorrows for us all ! Oh! What severe vis ita- =tations! yet, if God be pleas'd to sanctifye them to our souls, my belov'd freind and sister , how ought we to rejoice! rejoice in tribulation ! Sunday Even[in]g. Sep[tember]. 9th. Being prevented finishing my letter till now, I am to tell my dear sister, that [f.55v] I have since I began it \recd / two kind letters from my ever dearest mother , for which I beg you to present my affectionate duty and thanks. I find Mr A. did not acquaint her with the queries made to the Attorney G[enera]l6 and his answer s, if my eyes will permit7, I will transcribe them, but you must not mention to anybody but my mother about them. I am allow'd you'l see to remain here , a "reasonable time for the convenience of my affairs". I fear I cannot leave the place this fortnight. Some matters which are best talk'd over with my dear mother and sister (and that is \at present/ impossible) will detain me here. I have too great reason to think, when all is settl'd my poor youngest children will have but little to support them - but "God will provide ". I know not if Mr A. told my d[ea]r mother of the bond .8 Some years ago , my belov'd Husband thought proper to give me a parchment , which 6 The Attorney General at this time was William de Grey, fir st Baron of Walsingham (1719 –1781). He was related to the Cowpers, having married Mary Cowper (b. 1719), Maria’s sister -in-law, in 1743. 7 Maria had poor eyesight and as a child was sent to an oculist named Mrs King in Gravese nd where she learned to read and write. Roger Lonsdal e, Eighteenth -Century Women Poets: An Oxford Anthology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1989) p. 269. 8 A bond was an agreement for a financial penalty to be paid when certain conditions are met, i.e. a bondsman might commit to paying a widow money upon the death of her husband, as is the case in this instan ce. The bond here was written on parchment, a common practice until the seventeenth c entury. Most bonds after this date were written on paper, making this bond a little unusual. Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Zoe Screti; edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 3 he bid me "take care of, and lay it by, for it concern'd myself". It was open , but I never had the solicitude or curiosity to examine its contents, till within this week past, I recollect - =ed, and fetch'd it to my b[rothe]r Coll. Cowper9. We found it a deed of Gift of 1000 £ payable to me one month after my belov'd Cowper's decease, [f.56r] totally at my own disposal, and without deduction - by which act of goodness & generosity to unworthy me! I have somewhat to begin the world with - Oh my dear sister , and my dearest mother , I have unnumber'd things to tell you of - never was a time so frau ght with subject! but I must be silent till God is pleas'd to restore us to each others sight! docs.dcterms_abstract:
Acknowledging receipt of her letters from St. Jago and the Cape,
wishing her all felicity and reflecting on the course of her
experiences and preoccupations, e.g., outcome of war against the
Mahrattas and differences of people and climate from those at
Wareham; we doubt not you will find yourself agreeably settled and
happy in a circle of good acquaintances. The enclosed letter was
forwarded to me by your mamma to whom I have communicated every
intelligence I received of you. He reports a very severe winter and
posts and carriages stopped a long time on the roads.

Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.o x.ac.uk/about . 1 Penelope Maitland to Charlotte West 3 May 1783 SOURCE: Bodleian Libraries, MS. 6633, letters, 1783 –1805 May 3d. 1783 My Dear Miss Perry, _________ _ It is with great pleasure I congratulate you on your safe arrival once more in England, & being restor’d to the Company you of all others Wish to be in — that of your Fond Father — the joy of this meeting was, I Beleive , tout -a-fait mutuel — the hurry I wrote to him in yesterday with The receipt for his Agu e,1 (\&/ which I hope he this day receives) made me omit my congratulations to him ; however as they will be doubly ac= =ceptable thro’ your hands, I will forbear to regret the omission past. The many additional accomplishments you are return’d with, my Dear Charlotte, are so many additional motives of gratitude on Your side, & \attractives to/ affection on his — you are still a more delightful Compa = =nion than you were, tho’ this seem’d impossible. I am happy to be Assur’d from your [[ several words missing ]]2 likewise [re=] =turn’d in better health. may this & every other Blessing be continued To my dear Girl! to whose kindness I am most sensibly indebte d For the interest she takes in my welfare, & her concern express’d for 1 Illness involving fever and shivering. 2 The paper has been torn and then stitched back together again. Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear and Albert Sowerby -Davies ; checked by Tilly Guthrie ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.o x.ac.uk/about . 2 My health in particular. it has been in a very weak state for seve= =ral months past, but is much better within \the last/ 10 days. I now, with the Greatest Sincerity return you my th anks, for your extream kind And Entertaining letter from France. be assur’d your silence, tho’ a Subject of my regret , was none of my displeasure — as I had so much Confidence in your goodness, that I ascrib’d it wholly to the probable Delay of your receiving my letter, or your time being fully employ’d In the Convent, — not to your inclination or forgetfulness of your Absent Friend . the pleasing proofs your Sweet letter gave me that I was right in this opinion, demand my warmest acknowledgem en[ts] — A ma tr ês [[Cher Fille? ]] [page break ] your very Sensible & entertaining account of Mrs. Anville, make[s]3 Me Curious to hear her further history. the best part of it hitherto Seems to be, her not embracing the Roman Catholic religion, in w[hich] The Entire want of Charity is an indelible stamp of its Falshood, and Uncontrovertibly shews it sprang from Earth & never descended from Heaven . But indeed, On recollection I find I have paid it a com [=] =pliment \too great/ and should have been nearer the mark I beleive, ha[[ d I]]4 Gone a little lower than Earth for its Origin. I look upon it As one of the most Favorable omens to this Bad Age that the Papal Cause has receiv’d so many humiliating Checks from the 3 Final letter cut off by the end of the page. 4 The next letters are cut off by a small hole in the centre of a page. I wonder if The Convent “A L’ordre de Saint Benoit” escap’d the fate of the Rest, and likwise if the young Lady who came to your Convent with a determination to become a Religieuse, per = =sever’d in her intention. alas ! it is not walls of Brick or stone That Can inspire true Religion! – The rendering ourselves useless Is a very mistaken method of making u s Pious . The God of Wisdom & goodness has mark’d out a Brighter & a Beneficent Path, wch he has graciously made known to Erring Mortals, in That Word, w ch the Good Preists of the Romish Church take Care to Secrete from their deluded Followers ; well knowing those Heavenly Pages once in their hands, would soon open their eyes. — A Tho usand thanks to my dr. Girl for her kind wishes to [page break ] see her old Freind — who assues her they are return’d with Equal Warmth ; If, in some of my journeys to Town I can possibly obtain a Few minutes to Call in A -g-ll Street ,6 she may depend I will: but I Almost dispair on the Threshold of this Hope , as I now either go With the Governor of the Priory ,7 or into the Bloomsbury end of the Town. I will not however entirely relinquish the Idea, & in the mean 5 The Holy Roman Emperor, Joseph II (1741 –1790) who reigned from 1765 to 1790 . Will you not be surpriz’d [[to hear that ]]9 the sa me verita ble Mo[[p]] is still in being & in daily use? Decr. 1783 — Ma tr ês chere Fille I was favor’d with your very kind Letter of the 12. inst. Some days after date, occasion’d by the bad weather preventing my going or Sending to X X I return your many thanks, and am much oblig’d To you for informing me of the Foreign Journey being put off. I hope, most sincerely, you r Papa’s health will not suffer by passing the Winter under a Less Clement Sky. I beg my best Compl [imen ]ts to him, and assure him I am Very sorry for his Loss of so aimable a Freind as Sir Jno. Mitchell — & The shock his spirits \must/ have receiv’d from this melancho lly occas ion. the Attendance on the Last Hours of departing Freinds , strongly impress the mind, And point us to a Scene in which we are deeply interested. I read in The Papers Sir Jno’s. Death; and was quite at a loss to guess [[ several words ]]1 Papa had been set out already, or, wd. be wholly prevented g[[ several words ]] Event. I am greatly Concern’d to find his health is still not p[[ erfectly re=? ]] =cover’d. more of the Country air (tho’ Winter) I should strongly recommend. I hope you do not suffer him to set still too much, but persuade him to 1 Several words are omitted from this and the next two lines due to hist oric damage around where the seal would have been broken to open the letter . Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 Daily2 exercise. I have great Confidence in your persuasion. I return you my best thanks , my dear Charlotte, for your Kind solicitude for my health: it has again (I thank God) found Benefit from the Asses -milk. I feel stronger on my Lungs; which Seem absolutely to require this assistance. The Nun s3 are well, & Join in best Compl [imen ]ts. to your Papa & affectionate remembrance To yourself ; often wishing for you in some Impromptu dances on the Stair -Case of an Evening, Just by my door, where The Harpsichord [[ one word ]]4 nds. I imagin you have made [page break ] very good progress in m usic by this time , as in everything Else. how much do I wish to hear you! – and – to see you. This place is become a perfect Colony of Maitlands . there are, Between Le Chateau ,5 & the Governor’s Brother’s family (who live Near the Church) 17 or 18 of the Name. inshort, there is no Stirring without meeting one. the Captain6 has extreme ill Health, and his Lady very Closely attends upon him. It Is not a Custom In the Chateau e ver to go out of an Evening, so [[ several words ]]7 little intercourse in the Visiting way there , except of [[ several words ]] 9. yesterday Eve :[nin]g the Nuns were invited to a [[ several words ]] [w]ith their Couzins & were permitted to go, w [hi]ch made 2 An ink blot makes this more difficult to read. 3 Her nickname for her daughters , Penelope and Charlotte . 4 A flap of paper from the bott om of the page covers this word, which possibly reads ‘stands’. 5 Penelope Maitland referred to her house as ‘Le Chateau Blanc’ in her letters to Charlotte West. 6 This may refer to Captain Frederick Lewis Maitland RN (1730 –1786) , Penelope Maitland’s brother -in-law. Together with his brother, Lt Col John Maitland, he ha d been involved in the defence of Savannah in 1779, during the American War of Independence, the latter dying of malaria there. The milit ary connections of the Maitlands make it possible that some members of the family were looking for places to live on co nclusion of the Treaty of Paris in September 1783 , which meant a reduction in the armed forces. Captain Maitland had seven living children in December 1783, ranging from a few months to fifteen years of age , including the six -year -old Frederick Lewis Maitland who rose to the rank of Admir al, and who, when Captain of HMS Bellerophon , received the surrender of Napoleon Bonaparte in 1815 . 7 See footnote 1. My best apology for this bad scrawl, is indeed a very true one; viz: a weakness in my eyes, & one rather inflam’d about the Lids; I have had it some weeks & should be the more uneasy and alar m’d, but that numbers of other people have complain’d of the same here & elsewhere. I hope this find s my dr girl [page break ] In perfect health, and happy in seing her Papa much better Than when she wrote last. I inclose you a Puzzle; the history of wch Is, it represents a piece of ground in that shape, which a Father bequeath’d to 4 sons, to be d ivided in 4 Equal Parts Exact ly in the same shape — I am, my Dear Miss Perry your affectionate Freind & humble Servt. Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/abou t. 1 Penelope Maitland to Charlotte West 8 Sept ember 1787 SOURCE: Bodleian Libraries, MS . 6633, letters, 1783 –1805 Septr. 8 178[[7]] My Dear Charming Freind, A walk to x x was yesterday indeed repaid by the Receipt of your truly kind & most welcome letter of date 30. Augt. For which & a former of 16. Febry accept my Cordial thanks. How great is the pleasure of addressing you once more in England! I Congratulate you a thousand times over on your accomplishing The tedious , necessary absence , and now enjoying again the presence Of a Parent so deservedly belov'd, with all the additional good Reap'd from the two past years. How much greater still would be my pleasure at this time, could I frame the most distant Hope Of seing you my dear , dear miss Perry! Still I will hope – Perhaps in a moment unexpected I may Catch a glimpse & a word with you as you pass to the Farm -- while the Weather Lasts favorable, if Health permit, I may probably Walk to x x Once a week; I lately perform'd this march 2 days together, and Was much overcome indeed, it took double the number to re= =cover the effects of the fatigue. by which you will judge my Strength is not very great: but I have reason to be Thankful Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear, Jennifer Bunselmeier , and Ewa Wegrzyn; checked by Joshua Mascord and Laura Gonzalez ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/abou t. 2 I can walk it with ease when not too nearly repeated. The apologys you make my dr girl for not acquainting me Sooner of yr. arrival, do but reproach me the more for my long Delay in enquiring after that arrival : I expected, & also, ac= =knowledging your sweet lettr. from the Benedictines —alas! My Dear, in vain should I attempt to explain to you the many Things which \often/ withhold my hand even when my heart has a Thousand things to dictate. I Will leave myself to [your ] Goodness to pardon me, and when I think of that, I feel assur'd [ catchword ] [page break ] [as]sur'd of its effects. I have \often/ read & answered yr. \valued lettr/ in my mind, And am at a loss to express my sense of your kindness to one So without power to merit it my dr Miss Perry; particularly your enquiries after & solicitude f or my health. it is only the pleasure of Obeying a request of yours that I do more than mention it in the General. it is ever in a state that requires great care & attention and is quickly overthrown by any distress of mind or fatigue of body. The Former is less within my power to avoid than the latter, and Therefore I can only use all ye. means possible to repair the depreda= =tions. I was unfortunately depriv'd of one essentially necessary, for 4 months lately, the asses -milk; but I have again obtain'd It, and Am greatly better since. I doubt not your readily Believing what must have been the sufferings of my mind sometime Ago under the apprehensions for a week together of losing one of the Greatest supports & Comforts of my Life in my dear Ve sta, who Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear, Jennifer Bunselmeier , and Ewa Wegrzyn; checked by Joshua Mascord and Laura Gonzalez ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/abou t. 3 Was indeed all but gone with a violent Combination of Bilious and Jaundice Complaint. her Countenance wore so much the appear= =ance of death, that I Could hardly support looking at her, and Her strength was reduc'd in such a manner that on being taken out of bed for a few minutes to have it made, she fainted quite, and her Bilious Complaint return'd wth. such violence, she was Oblig'd to be hurr ied into bed with all expedition. I am happy To say, she is now entirely res tor'd to health & looks, & joins wth Vitula in every affection ate remembrance & wish to yourself, and With me in best Compl[ imen ]ts. to monsr. votre Per e, congratulating him Not less than yourself, on your return to England. I imagin his Stay at Edmonton will be short, as the Militia are soon to be Reduc’d to their state of Non -Entity again. [ Oh that ] I had been [page break ] so Fortunate as to be at or near the Cottage when he paid it lately, a reconnoitring Visit! one extream fine Evening in Last week I & Vesta walk'd all about it, and talk 'd over former Times -- never did I see anything so lovely as the fields full of Rowings, \gilded by/ the Evening Sun. it is a Charming spot! & happy wd It make us to have the present inhabitants give it again into Some hands we Could mention , with the Liberty annex'd of Free access to them . the House is in a ruinous condition, & Likely I think to drop to the ground before the Law -suit is Setl'd between the two Contending Parties, Mr Church and Scurrard . the Old Clerk & his Family, mean time, are delight ed Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear, Jennifer Bunselmeier , and Ewa Wegrzyn; checked by Joshua Mascord and Laura Gonzalez ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/abou t. 4 With their situation; I do not unfrequently pay them a visit of half an hour; they are good Sort of People, chatty & very Well Bred, & I am all the time endulg'd with looking at a Place I have a Partiallity for, and objects which call others to My reme mbrance. Mrs. Whithal has all her life been a great Reader, & I must confess the girls & I find more entertainment In her Conversation & her old very Sensible Mother's, than in Most of the Lady Neighbours here. however, these visits of ours there are all in secret, as the fear of the Small -Pox is so Extream, that we are prohibited entering any house where there are young Children, as the Idea of Them & the Small -Pox Is inseparable. Vitula was truly oblig'd by your sweet lettr. & wishes for abi= =lity to answer it in Coin , she is I beleive summoning all Her French to this end, but it is likely it will be more than half. In Mother -Tongue . you mention'd, my dr girl, an intended request to your kind Papa for a 6 month ’s residence in Italy; I Do not wo nder if he Could not part with you for so long an addition [page break ] of absence. as you understand the Language enough to Read It, and are so perfect a mistress of French, I think you will not much miss the conversing in Italian. I must enquire How goe s on music? Your Names sake still improves, without any reason for her doing so except her love & genius for it, For she owes little to Practise & less to instruction. Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear, Jennifer Bunselmeier , and Ewa Wegrzyn; checked by Joshua Mascord and Laura Gonzalez ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/abou t. 5 You diverted me much with informing me of my ridiculous Mistake about Miss Harris, whom my Fancy had reduc’d to Her Childhood again. but, my dear Miss Perry, when the title of Miss is continued \to the / 50th. year, one is easily led into the Mis- take. – As you were pleas’d with the account of Sunday Schools, yo ur Pleasure will be I dare say encreas’d to hear of their won = =derful prosperity. I read an extream good sermon of Doctr. Kaye’s lately preach’d to the Association for the Charity [A]t St. Martin ’s in the Fields, where in he computes the number Of children now taught throughout this realm, att 200,000 – A Cause of unspeakable thankfulness to God whose Evident Work it is! – the above sermon gives one of the most distinct Idea Of the institution, & the important benefits of it. we have Two Sunda y Schools here. one of which has Mrs. Williams for Its Patroness, the other Mrs. Vaughan. the Teaching Mistresses Are – Dame Fuller and Suky Slight – the latter I bel eive you remember being rather a remarkable little figure. the former has obtain’d a name amo ng us of , Mrs. Proviso . as she seldom Speaks 10 words without introducing that word “with a Proviso” – so that I think whatever her scholars forget, they will Be perfect in this ornament of speech. it is to be regretted That more able instruc tors cannot be found for this great & good work. [page break ] Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear, Jennifer Bunselmeier , and Ewa Wegrzyn; checked by Joshua Mascord and Laura Gonzalez ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. Mr. Townsend. it is no small Piece of self -denial to be not to go, but the smell of the Paint is So excessive, I dare not hazard my Lungs. the La ne towards x x is much improve’d, the opposite Bank having Been transform’d into a sort of Garden by its owner. – I will only add in the hope of hearing From my dear girl when [leisuie] makes It perfectly convenient, that I am With Sincere affection Hers Constance a thousand intentions have Detained this till Septr.11--. and a reason about the Postman has detain'd It on ‘till the 15 -th- I am just setting out with Vitula for -- ------ Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear, Jennifer Bunselmeier , and Ewa Wegrzyn; checked by Joshua Mascord and Laura Gonzalez ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. The length of my last1 might well Induce you to wish me silent a little longer, but I am desirous to Communicate to your Papa2 My having written to Epsom3 to Recommend the Argus , & to beg its Interest may be Promoted. I should with the utmost pleasure endeavour to e xtend it in This place as you mention, but, my Love, you know this is Wholly out of my Power , as what I only am entrusted wth Privately I cannot recommend Publickly . This, proceeding from the dif = =ficulty’s of my Peculiar Situation, will I am sure Apologize for Me on this head. I shal long to know how it goes on in London &c and hope for the pleasure of hearing from you tht The former dissapointment is likely to be fully made Amends For in this new attempt. My best Compliments wait on yr 1 Could this be the letter dated 16 March 1789, which was of considerable length? In this letter Penelope talked about The Argus and Sampson Perry . 2 Samson Perry , father to Charlotte West (née Perry ). 3 Underlined words in the transcription correspond to underlined words in the manuscript. The same, ma Très Chere , pray Present to Mr. West; my Sincere acknowledgments are re = =turn’d for the most obliging attention to my Son, and For your kind Sympathy on a late Vexatio us Dissapointmt. He is at present with us, well in health, I thank God! and Desires his Comp l[imen]ts. Whenever the next occasion happens of Military promotion, It will be seen how far my present fears are Well -grounded or not. I own (and not without very strong rea = =sons from something I lately heard from Good Authority) I cannot But apprehend a Certain Viscount’s Name in the Opposition, (Couzin To A —g—s4,)5 is of much diservice to him in this Point, though in All others it wd probably be the very Contrary. All of that Name Are \too likely to be/ involv’d in One Suspicion – and a Person here not appear = =ing att Court & Levées &c corroborate the Suspicion which Must be so detrimental to him. You say “many things have happen’d to you, my dr friend, Since you wrote last, th’o too immaterial to relate .” — believe Me, when I tell you, nothing could be th ought immaterial By me, in which you were concern’d. I will only add on this Head, that I hope nothing may happen to lessen that hap= =pines s I so ardently wish you to possess. your health I 4 Augustus, Penelope Maitland’s son. 5 The brackets, in a darker ink, seem to have been added later. I am quite an Enthusiast on these Charms of [– the Country] \Nature/. My Nuns6 join in Compl[imen]ts, Love & every best wish; we have Reason to be thankful that our healths are tolerably good; V: \and V:/ Are almost incessantly with the G ——7. Tho' I with cause regret having so little of their Company, it is peculiarly happy for me That I have a strong Partiallit y for Solitude, since so great a Share falls to my lot. They are at present all walk’d up to pay a Visit at Mrs. L —'s. The Chariot being Useless On Account of a horrid Vicious horse which has a thousand times hazarded their necks, and about a fortnight ago, was within A Straw’s breadth on overturning the G - & poor d [ea]r Vitula in the Lane , in the Sigh t of some Company (who were on a walk hither) & who Were so much affected with the danger, they did Not wholly recover themselves the whole day. I have never Set my foot in the chariot these two years, nor ever intend it ‘Till other horses are procur’d; but my daily Terror s for th < > 8 Fright & danger the dr Nuns alternately undergo, are inexpressible. 6 This is the name Penelope Maitland uses for her daughters. Your generous mind & kind heart have made you rob yourself to enrich them. this Circumstance we regret. The Nuns inform you I Have been ill. the complaint was Bilious & so severe on Tuesday \evening,/ tha t They continued staying by me ’till one o’ Clock Wednesday morning, with Most tender & affectionate attention. A Gentleman being in The Parlour , (who Had Come from Town on Regimental Business & was to sleep here) detain’d the G––l longer up than usual, and the Nuns wd. not go to their beds while I Continued out of mine & so ill. I had a very indifferent night indeed w [he]n. I Could get to bed, & was so reduc’d in strength, & \in/ such painful lassitude In every Limb when I arose about ½ past 7 the next morning, that I Was oblig’d to keep my room all day. I sincerely pitied all that might Be expos’d to it! — — I hope, my dear second Charlotte (for you tell Me & give me the pleasing assurance you and Mr. W. Look on me as a Little related to you in the Maternal Character – Oh that I had those Kindnesses in my power which might render me deserving \that title &/ the favor you do Me!) that you spent a pleasant week in the the Country, & found ben efit To your health: that you saw Lady Lyttelton ,1 & that she behav’d to Your wish. did not she discover all was not right between you My dear, & your Father? Augustus says, he met Mr. West, and Was sorry to hear there was no alteration. s o far then he, & the two Nuns know: that there is at present no intercourse between him & You — and I was oblig’d to subjoin the Cause was S [uke]y. P.ac.2 as they Appear’d startl’d, & might think it was some fault or miscounduct in my dear freind towards her once -endulgent Father. I hope in this I Did not go farther than you wish, but I was eager to acquit you in their Idea. [page break] I never hear d anything so audacious as her behaviour about the Goods you were to send for from his house — the glass particularly. The manner in which you inform’d him was perfectly right. how I la = 1 Proba bly Caroline Bristow, wife of Sir William Lyttelton, seventh bart. , baron Westcote (1724 –1808). 2 Susannah (Sukey) Patience (1756 –1813) , who married Sampson Perry in Oct ober 1809. I am very truly Concern’d at so unhappy a reverse of the scene , and most earnestly wish \& yet hope,/ a happier may in time Take place! Doubtless she will do all in her power to prevent it, that she may mono = =polize all his affections & money. but the Power of Providence is above All, and whoever commits their cause to that in a way of strict duty , Will surely \find/ their happiness in so doing sooner, or, later. Pray my dr may I ask what is become of a young gentleman nam’d Augustus — another nam’d William — once in the care of Wm. Per’s[?] Wife In Whetstone Lane — I also understood, there were several other children?3 the Transient glimpse you had of yr. I am sorry to find that horrid paragra =\=ph/ Originated there, as it too much confirms me in the opinion I at Once form’d of it by its style, that it was in the opposition in = =terest. the exhorbitant price you mention being given for Them on the above paragraph being in it, confirms it yet more. I am glad yr Father met with no farther consequences: I Cannot tell you my dr. Freind, how greiv’d I am he should be inclin’d to the Party . pray tell me, if I am wrong. What, my dear, was the particular Subject of those Numbers you ex = =press ’d a wish I should see? but which I know not how to get. [page break ] I am happy to hear so good an account of your house -keeping, your Attention to Oeconomy & the good fruits you have already found in being Able to adjust the little embarrasments contracted in less prudent moments , Truly excusable in so early a season of Life: I admire the principle yt [that] Led you to adjust them, and doubt not, my aimable Freind , this, & the Un= =derstanding you are blest with far more matur’d than many of your Sex of maturer years, Will henceforth have their due influence in Preserving you from occasions of Uneasiness - let it be Engrav’d on yr Sensible mind , ma três chere , that one of the Great secrets of peace , Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear, Carlos Fonseca Grigsby , Alexandra Sheldon, and Jade McGlynn ; checked by Jenni fer Bunselmeier and Ewa Wegrzyn; c hecked and edited by Mike Webb. Pleasure of the truest kind, must & will follow the inward plea = =sure of an approving conscience . what we designedly & ultimately Spend on Pleasure as Our Object , generally ends in regret & anxiety. What we spend on Prudence , ends in Pleasure. you are happy in Each other , and therefor e need not put yourselves to the ex pence of Seeking happiness in the Worlds expensive Follie s & Fashions; & where It never can be found. you are also most agreably situated as to Your Neighbourhood among so many kind relations, which I am rejoyc [’d] To hear - and I hope your Fathers sad pr ognostications when he Heard you were gone to House =keeping, and which Doubtless arose from His Idea of your unexperienc’d youth , will be so happily revers’d, That the Accounts of your Happiness & Prudence, & good Management May attract his admiration and compel him, by the most agreable Force to reward it; for he has too much sense not to approve what is right. Tuesday Octr. 6th. Vesta is gone in the Chariot, & Vitula is at work by me , having a little sorethroat & a very great cold. her Kind love & compliments beg a place here. I now proceed , to [page break ] Speak , on the instructive & interesting Subject of the venerable old Gentle = =man’s death of which you give me so sensible & Awful an account. I call it interesting as well as instructive, my sweet Freind , for tho’ the Person was unknown to me, yet all are interested in Death - and every New instance of Mortality, holds out a fres h lesson of instruction to us, Who — “whate’er we do, where e’er we are, are travellling to the grave “ — As a most beautiful Hymn of Doctr. Watts5 expresses it . it was a Very solemn office to set by & watch the retreating spirit — and o h how Beyond measure awful the thought, that when the scene was clos’d here, And nothing remain’d but the Breathless clay, the Soul in full Vigour of all its Faculties, no more to Cease from Existence, either of happiness Or Misery, was enter’d on a World of Spirits — summon’d before its great Creator & Redeemer, immediately to receive the doom which the Last Day, will not alter , but \only / confirm and compleat for ever! I never heard anything more surprizing than the sudde n return of his 5 Isaac Watts (1674 –1748) , Congregational minister and hymn writer . Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 7 health & strength just preceding his dissolution — It appears the violent Effort of Nature conflicting with her last Tremendous Enemy — The Burial Service of our church is surely the finest composition in the world , So far from melancholly , that I think it contains the most animating Cordials against the Fears & horrors of Death. — I have been quite shock’d with the awful account of Ld Huntingdon’s6 sudden removal from this world; Especially as I know he liv’d the greatest part of his Lif e an Unbeliever ; I hope he did not die so! but that the unwearied Prayers of that most Excellent Saint his Mother, (whom I have had the honor of intimately Knowing many, many years7) have been heard on his Behalf. — Truely it may be said, that if his Ldship never Preach’d in his Life, he Preach’d a very solemn sermon at his death — The manner of which Call’d upon all who saw it, and calls upon all who hear of it, to live as Creatures that must die, & know not when they may die. docs.dcterms_abstract: Maitland mentions meeting at Barnett Assembly. She encourages Charlotte West to read James Hervey's 'Meditations on a flower garden', which is believed to be a reference to 'Reflections on a flower-garden' in James Hervey's 'Meditations and Contemplations' (1746–7; rev. edn., 1748). Maitland mentions also a hurricane which caused a woman and man to suffer physical ailments; comments on the hostilities occurring between the Times and the Argus newspapers. Lastly, she mentions a recipe for ginger wine, which she recommends as a summer drink. [Eileen Jakeway and Peri Sipahi]

Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.b odleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Penelope Maitland to Charlotte West 20 February 1791 SOURCE: Bodleian Lib raries, MS. 6633, letters, 1783 –1805 20th Febry 1791 My Dear Charlotte, Twice I think we have been writing to each other at the same time, & Our letters must have cross’d on the road. probably it will happen a Third time , and I shal receive your new address, while this finds You on the point of leaving Mrs. Turings. A thousan d \thanks/ my dear for Your last kind letter. I do not wonder you were press’d to remain With your Freind another month. I envy her happiness, which is Very ill -natur’d of me, you’ll say. I sent a thousand Blessings to my dear Boy on the day on which his Birth day was To be celebrated. may he long live to the Comfort of his Parents and his Maker’s glory, & to know Him and his Redeemer & Saviour ! I sent likewise Sincerest wishes, my dr freind, for the unallay’d Joy & Comfort of the Day . particularly that your Father’s presence & Kindness might give your anxious heart the Enjoyment of the Happy Occasion & the pleasing Society. \as/ you may be sure you have awaken’d my interested feelings on your account, by wht. You say, or rather intimate of “telling me more bye & bye,” and Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear , Eileen Jakeway , and Peri Sipahi; checked by Greta Galeotti and Arunima Amar ; edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.b odleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 of the Letter on some important Business you had written to Monsr votre Père, I trust you will kindly Explain when proper And Convenient to you to do so. I hope he will assist you in the Expence of S ettling in your new Habitation, & make still easier Your little Rest. I long to know where it is, & am glad to find It is so near Town. May Health & Content (those Sovereign Blessings of Life! ) long attend you \& yours/ in it! your employments Will all be of the Quiet & Healthful kind; & that of bringing Up your Sweet Boy, a most delightful & improving one. the only & sure way to obtain Power to perform any good, any duty, is My dear, to ask of God. the Wisest without this must want still \wisdom &/ Instruction. I am sure I am a poor Ignorant Mortal, & can help you but little. Yet as in my own experience with a young family I have [page break ] necessarily made some observations, & also from seing others, I will When time permits set down a few of them for your pe rusal. it is Totally impossible to explain to you, my belov’d freind, how much I long have \been/ & am in want of leisure, as also the Dr Nuns1. who send their most affectionate remembrance & Wishes —their healths are Better at present. the Pint of Sweet Butter milk goes down Cordially every Morning with Vesta. They have lately adopted Chocolate (made thin ) for Breakfast, and they express finding great benefit. it is extreamly no u= =rishing & wholsome Made thin, & very unwholsome when thick . Our 1 As per the donor’s summary, Charlotte’s daughters Vesta and Vitula. Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear , Eileen Jakeway , and Peri Sipahi; checked by Greta Galeotti and Arunima Amar ; edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.b odleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 3 Military came to us yesterday, and is gone this Evening (Viz: ye 21st inst2) To the Barnett assembly. I have not had opportunity to ask him About my Freinds in Sloane Street. Mr. W. was very kind to call on him: It appears by the end of your letter my Dear that you saw him somewhe \re/ I hope he call’d on Mr. W. and met you both at home. my heatlh, I have Infinite cause of thankfulness, continues far better than I Could expect; Tho’ my looks speak otherwise. I am totally witho ut my long experien’cd Cordial, the asses milk, & likely to remain so. -- I am sorry to find Hostillities are going on between the Times & the Argus . the latter will Have much trouble & expence I should apprehend. Pray my Dear did I ever give \you/ the receipt to make Ginger Wine (as it is most improperly call’d I think, being much more of the Cyder or Perry kind) it is a most delightful Summer Beverage. very wholsome & Easily, as well as Cheaply made. it may be drank even when a Person is pritty ho t, with safety, which hardly any liquor (wine & .c excepted ) Can. it is full of Fix’d air, which you know is all the fashion Now —and drinks with the very spirit of Champaign. the Nuns & I are immoderately fond of it. I believe I told you in my last of a poor Lady at Hampstead who in the First dreadful Hurricane we had, fainted away with fright, and Soon after recovering herself, was sitting up in her Bed, when on ye. Thunder beginning, she sunk down on her Pillow & expir’d. a more Extraordinary effect that storm had on a Man, who being awaken’d 2 Since the letter was initially dated 20 February 1791, this parenthetical reveals she wrote the letter over the course of at least two days. Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear , Eileen Jakeway , and Peri Sipahi; checked by Greta Galeotti and Arunima Amar ; edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.b odleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 4 [page break ] By the extraordinary combination of Elements, concluded it the Day of Judgment, and fell into such Convictions of an Evil Conscience, that it wrought upon his Body such illness, as requir’d the immediate Help of the Physician , who, however pronounc’d his aid would be In vain: the unahppy man us’d all the Language of utter dispair, and his Wife coming to the Bedside and asking him what could be the Cause, and how long he had had s uch dreadful thoughts &c he stretch’d out his hand towards her & said in an audible voice, “You, ever since I knew you.” he then confess’d, He had married His own Brother’ s Widow ; (they had 7 children) he cont inuing in the same agonies of mind, Religious Aid was call’d in, and a Man of great abilities was sent for: who after much prayer & Converse &c it pleas’d God mercifully to Ca lm the wounded spirit, [-and] to vouchsafe grace to repentance & Faith , & the the Man died In Hope . Judge what his Agonies Must have been, in so short [mnw] a space of Time, to bring his Body to the grave! Oh my dear, What an Awful Warning to every heart is this to make Life a Constant preparation for death! I assure you this was a fact. remember my belov’d charlotte, not to transmit any thing out of my letters to the Paper , as it must betray from Whence it Came. a Minister too was my author for this little [-accou ]\history/ , and would not be pleas’d to have it made pub= =lic probably. I have lost my third Grand child , And obtain’d a Daughter -in-Law Since last I wrote. Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear , Eileen Jakeway , and Peri Sipahi; checked by Greta Galeotti and Arunima Amar ; edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.b odleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 5 I have been interrupted my Dear 20 times at least from the time I began this scrawl , which will apologize I hope for all its many defects. Do you remember a group of Tall beautiful Elms just on a little rising Bank Nearly opposite our Blue gate the Centr e one has long lean’d a good deal towards the Road, and the late storms increas’d this evidently. I said frequently [page break ] It was most dangerous. but no body would be persuaded of it. 2 days ago it Fell in a moment, Snapp’d off Close at the root. Several \People/ had pass’d in the very direction in which it fell, and it was a Signal Providence none Were hurt. It is the nature of Elms to have a very little root, & to grow very high. which makes them ever dangerous to be near a house or frequ ented Path. a circumstance to to be regretted, as they are lovely Trees for Shade & Beauty. – your little Garden will Yield you I hope both health & pleasure. nothing can Make one enjoy a Garden more I think than reading “Herveys meditations on a Flower Garden.”3 we Enjoy everything as we ought and were undoub tedly Design’d to do, when every Creature leads us up to 3 James Hervey, Meditations and contemplations ran to numerous editions. I am Constrain’d to subscribe myself In haste, with best respects to Mr. West, My dear, dear Freind Yours most affectionately, L’Abbesse Your cough I hope No more molests you & that You are entirely well Answer’d the 11th April 17914 4 In another hand, presumably that of Charlotte West .

Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Penelope Maitland to Charlotte West 10–22 May 1791 SOURCE: Bodleian Libraries, MS. 6633, letters, 1783 –1805 May 10 th 1791 Mr Dear Freind, Your kind Letter of the 11.th of April, should have sooner been ac= =knowledg ’d, had not an abundance of Hindra nces prevented. accept my best thanks, & my sincerest congratulations on the recovery of your little Angel. you judg’d extre amly right to delay the information of the Inocu= =lation ’till accompany’d with the successful Event. this, & every mercy , Will I trust have the happy effect of drawing up your mind to the Divine Author. daily should we consider our ince ssant dependence on Him for all our comforts ! and Pray also t hat our Hearts and best affec= =tions may be plac’d on the only comfort that cannot fail us , which is Himself . I am very glad, my dear Love, that you followed the advice, and comply’d with the wishes of Mr. West & your father , & That the sweet Child had so little to suffer from the distemper. he Was I hope thoroughly physick’d after it, and will remain in Perfect health to your comfort. Believe me, me trés chere; there Never can be any apology necessary for telling me all particulars about him. I regr et to an inexpresible degree not being able to see and hear him, — how truly kind it was in Mrs. Turing to detain you Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear and Leon Hughes; checked by Tilly Guthrie ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 My dear ’till the anxious scene was over! I form ye. most pleasing Ideas of her friendly character , & rejoyce in your having such a Freind. the affair of the House was a provoking one indeed. I am glad you are quit of such a Landlord, th o’ at a dear rate; And hope you will be made ample amends at Richmond. I beg You will give me the fullest description of your house there and Its situa tion; likewise if you have the whole or only part. May Health & every Ble ssing attend you & yours there! it is a Charming place, but too much built -up. you give the great pleas= =ure my dr in the account of your Father’s Returning kindne ss To you, and fondne ss for his little Grandson. you will allow [page break ] I ever encourag’d you to hope for this in the Perseve rance of your Duty to him. it is indeed an invariable rule in all cases , to Keep on in that Path, however difficult and discouraging it may appear. his kind presents of Furniture will I hope be follow ’d by more of other kind s \ and that / the Law -suit1 being well ended May leave it more in his Power. — The Lady who went to France, is I Imagin lon g since return’d . I am astonish’d any one ventures them= =selves there, in a scene of universal horror & anarchy! they are an Infatuated People, sorely visited of Heaven for their extream of every Wickedne ss, and seem at present given up for reprobate minds. Boasting of Liberty and enslaving their King! Sr. Jos: Andrews 1 Presumably a reference to the ‘Hostillities … going on between the Times & the Argus ’ mentioned in Penelope Maitland’s letter dated 20 Feb ruary 1791. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 3 Lately come from thence, told a Lady of my acquaintance, that there was not the least Trace left in France of Religion of any kind. they are trampling on all Laws divine & hum an. May every Nation take such a due Horro r at them as to go To the extreamest opposite to all their \ iniquitous / Proceedings. The sweet dear Cottage2 I hear has got a new Proprietor, whose Name is Miller , to whom Mr Scurrard has sold it. I hope he Will repair the House, which must otherwise be soon uninhabitable. It is \ a / remarkable Place for its short stay with every Po ssessor. about 7 different People have had it within these 10 years. this is ow= =ing I am told to the greatne ss of the Farm -rent. as to our Green Which was so uncommonly beautiful, they are Spoiling it in every Possible way. Millions of Bricks have been made & Burn’d and are still making upon it, tho’ the Church is nearly Comple ated. And they are also digging for gravel all over it, by which Means \ severa l of / the Trees are distroy’d; one most Beautiful Elm thrown down of 6 that stood in a row not far from our house — and they are Now digging just before our Front Gate. I suppose my dr you have read & heard Enough of the Gunning affair3 to [Page Break] Make you sick of it. wherefor e will only say, that if you & Mr. W. have read Mrs G_ _’s Pamphlet, I strongly recommend it to you to read Capt . Bowen’s . ’till I 2 Presumably she refers to the cottage where the Perrys once lived in Totteridge. 3 Elizabeth Gunning was rumoured to be betrothed to the ma rquess of Blandford, heir to the duke of Marlborough. They do however dis cover a History, in regard to Mrs. & Miss G: that I beleive Must stand for ever Unparalel’d in the Annals of time for Deceit , and Perjury . Miss G:’s solemn Oath , and Solemni zing \ it / with the Preface, that Nothwithstand her youth, she fully felt the Weight of the Transaction with Regard to its Consequences in Both Worlds , “4 engag’d me entirely to Credit Her, and among all the Parties, I Set her down for Innocent , injur’d & Unfortunate . But I am struck with horror for her Condition in Both Worlds (the next especially) to find on indisputable Evidence, she is perjur’d in all She swor e to; and not content with perjuring herself, did actually offer A Bribe of 20 £ a year for Life to a servant if he would take a false Oath To Conceal what she had done of giving him a forg’d letter to deliver to her Father as from the D. of Marlbro’ . — in short the Lies of Mother & Daughtr Terrefye me, and equally astonish me ! — what are Birth, Education & all the charms of Beauty & accomplishment, without the grace of God ! Whatever we are depriv’d of leaving to our Children of this world’s goods, Let it be ever our daily pra yer & Endeavour, my dear freind , to leave ’em Posses’d of the true riches , the Grace and Blessing of God ; we may then Live & die in perfect ease about them. but in the Modern education, this is the last thing thought of, or, rather I may say more Properly, left wholly Out. If you read in the old Testament, my dr Charlotte, you will Find that God commanded his People to teach their Children the 4 There is no counterpart to this mark, so it is impossible to tell if she intended to open or close a quotation. This injunction Equally belongs to us: and if we wish to have comfort In our children or obedience from them , we must lay the foundation in The Knowledge , Fear & Love of God early sown in their hearts. [page break ] In all they see and admire , they should be taught that God, who Made them , gives them all; they should be continually taught Lessons of Truth , Mercy and Charity . the contrary to these are [-Very] \ too / easily, and too generally inculcated on their tender minds, by The most simple & trivial means, of the consequence of which, People Are not aware. when the little Innocents commit any mischief, It is often suggested to them by their Maid or Nurse, to lay the fault on Some one else, which soon hardens them in Deceit . — the suffering Them to Hu rt animals or in sects of any kind, teaches them Tyranny and Cruelty — and as to all objects of distre ss in the human species, They should be ever learn’d to feel for them in the tenderest manner, And to delight to relieve them — and to look upon Money as given for this purpose of all others. to discourage the vice of Covetousne ss in the Love of money, is another necessary le sson to instil into them , And also that most horrid one of Revenge ; which (as all other Evils Being, deeply implanted in our fallen Nature) requires the Earliest Remedy . how constantly do we hear people bid children beat any thing or Person, when they happen to get a hurt o r fall, they Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear and Leon Hughes; checked by Tilly Guthrie ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 6 Will tell them to beat the floor, the Table , or some body near — what is this but inculcating this devilish Passion? and teaching them Ever after to return Evil for Evil — in direct contradiction to their Saviour’s Command. now, my dear, as it is evident that by small Hints , trifling examples & the most simple methods , Children are Taught and increas’d in sin & evil, so by the same we may & ought To teach, continually Instruct, and impre ss them with all good . and this Latter being the most opposite to their Natures, is certainly the most difficult, requiring a ll our attention & Pains. the other , Alas! is swimming with the stream — the work is done to our hands, And only wants improvement , which is the fatal mischeif Parents m ust Study to avoid, and Counter -Act, as they value their children’s souls and their own, for doubtle ss if they have to answer for the [page break ] Bodily welfare of their offspring, much more for their souls. It is singularly our Duty to teach them the highest reverence for The scriptures: daily, when they are old enough, to make them read a Portion of them, and to comment upon them in a plain & f orcible Manner , which may in their future Lives be “a Lamp to their Ways “and a Light to their Paths, and as David says, “that the word of “God may be so hid in their heart, that it may be a Powerful restraint “from their sinning against him.” I know a Lady of Fashion, very religious, who brought up her Children to look on reading the Bible as such a high honor and Happine ss (as doubtle ss it is to all) that their Punishment when they Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear and Leon Hughes; checked by Tilly Guthrie ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. May 21 .st Saterday night. My dear freind, I have \ been / oblig’d to lay this by from many hindrances And one has been this whole week, my being much indispos’d With a violent Cough, which all attention & the Posture of writing Much encrease — I caught it on Monday Evening last by a Walk out I could no way avoid with some Company, and I Have Never been out since: the weather having too been dan= = gerously cold. I beleive the Origin of my cough & Hoarsene ss Was before the time I here mention; on Saterday se[n]’night I Most imprudently walk’d out in the Evening as far only as Mrs. G — to thank her for a favor done me, and there was one of the strongest Blights I ever saw, the whole air was render’d thick & unwholsome, & I was Hoarse soon after . [page break ] I am taking a variety of recipes, but alas! am without my Cordial, the a sses-milk — the prospect is very distant to having it. I have an equal opinion of Sweet Butter Milk, but not an Equal liking of the taste. I think the Philosophers of the age must be puzzl’d to account for What we have for above this we ek daily experienc’d, that the South West Wind has blown as Cold as the North East. I have indeed frequently remark’d it at times for this year or two past. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Penelope Maitland to Charlotte West 4 February 1792 and 29 April 1792 SOURCE: Bodleian Libraries, MS. 6633, letters, 1783 –1805 Sloane Street No 5. — Feb.ry 4th. 1792 My Dear Freind — I hope you got safe the letter I sent immediately on the receipt of your Last According to your request to make you easy for its due arrival . — I should sooner have follow’d it with another, as I then promis’d , but have Prevented by much illne ss. I am just recovering, thr’o the divine mercy, From a Six weeks confinement to my room . and I bless God, am so Well recover’d , as to beleive I should be quite so, if the spring was more Advanc'd , that I could venture into the Air; which I have not the Smallest imagination of doing , before the Sweet Month of April ; for My suffering s have been so great and various in this illne ss, that I Think I shal be more than ever a slave to the dread of catching cold. How I caught this, was astonishing, as I had not been out for Days, from extream Caution to save myself up for church on Xmas Day. On the monday before it, which was the 19 .th of Dec.r, I was sitting at work in our very hot Parlor after dinner, near Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear and Leon Hughes; c hecked and edited by Mike Webb. I felt such Inten se sudden Coldne ss all over me, inside & out, that I could not Conceive po ssible in so warm a situation — it baffl’d every means Tried, and continued in a most painf ul manner all night & Part of next day — a Head -Ach, sickish stomach, sorethroat, and soon after, an Excruciating Rheumatism in my right Shoulder and arm, which depriv’d me of the use of it, and Continued near a Week day & night; wn it subsided there, it Seiz’d my right Wrist & hand, & was quite an agony indeed. I then could neither use hand or arm . the great lo ss of which , None can tell but those who experience it. and perhaps it is Right we should experience. Sometimes a suspension of our Blessings, that we may learn to be more thankful for them, And our Obligation of Perpe tual Praise to the bestower of them. I had a very great inconvenience in being drest & undrest by My Maid, a most awkward feeling, especially to me who never Can endure the least a ssistance of the kind, except only to fix up My hair behind to a cushion — tho’ I have regain’d the use [page break ] — Sunday April ye 29 1792 — 1 ‘Governor ’, one of the terms she uses for her husband Sir Alexander Maitland. Accept my sincere, tho’ tardy ackn owledgements my Dear Ch. I receiv’d Heart -felt delight & satisfaction in the good account yo Sent me of your own and Family’s Healths, which I hope still and May long continue , & that your Nursing may conduce to this end . I am much pleas’d with the description of my Robust little Boy, and The Beauty of his New Brother, but cannot allow him to be Handsommer than my Charles .1 — th’o I am not acquainted with The Parties , I wish all Happin ess to the marriage of Mr. Innes & 1 Charles Edward West, Charlotte West’s first child b. 1790 . I beg my belov’d sister will not be uneasy if she hears not punctully from me as as usual, the dif = =ficulty of conveyance, not always knowing where to direct to Henry will sometimes occasion delay - and at this moment I cannot say whether at Ham , in Town, or at Cole Green , so venture at all events to address you sans frank . I did not half answer your delightful, entertaining, \long / letter nor can I now, for want of time. How in every corner of the globe , I find business starting up on all sides, is wonderful! But so it is. I have met wi th some charming manuscript poems of W.C.s1 a lady has lent me her barn to transcribe . This is one thing that engrosses me at present, when I am in my chamber. My own poor poems, I find have made their way into Yorkshire! May God’s blessing accompany them, and He shall have all the Glory, \if any good be done ./ I brought with me many old papers to look over, which is a matter of serious employment . Will you my dear sister contrive a way to lay out ½ a g[uine]a for me for P. Lewis. It quite distresses me, not to be 1 William Cowper (1731 –1800), poet, cousin of Maria Cowper . Perhaps he will also convey the parcel to her. I bless God for the continuance of your truly precious health —my own is purely, was it not for the rhumatism , which so attacks my shoulder nightly at different hours — but I am taking medicine, which I trust will be b lest to the removal of so unpleas ant a companion, or patience to bear the divine will! Surrounded with comforts and mercies as I am, it is fit I should have something to re = =mind me of my dependance. Oh! For a faithful confidence in the Father of Mercies! He knows what is best for his chil= =dren at all times. I have experienc’d great deadness of spirit , and smallness of faith, since I came to this place . This is the needs -be I dare say , and the seldom opportunities of ordinances, (for w hich I mourn) shews me how greatly I need them , and how my graces wither without ’em! The Lord supply my heart with that grace, the means of which I am not in a way here \much / to enjoy. Only church once a week & once in the day. The family pew so far from the minister I hear but very imperfectly what is deliver’d from an excellent Gospel preacher. We all din’d lately at the house of a good clergyman and [fol. 72r] his wife. After tea he read us an excellent serm [on], shew’d us a small old prayer book of K. Charles 1st own manual of prayers, out of which he read to us many interesting passages. docs.dcterms_abstract: Penelope discusses small pox in her area, her daughter's poor health, and her own (an other daughter's) good health. She expresses concern for Charlotte's father, who was recently ill, and she sends her best wishes well for Charlotte's children. She discusses some recent deaths in her village.

I feel 1 The address and date have been cut off. I have lately Thought that in time by means of your becoming intimate with Mrs French, there might be a probability of your paying a visit here openly — let us still hope my dr freind, in the Events of Time. and Mean time , whatever you convey by post is perfectly safe, and shall be Kept inviolably secret as far you Enjoin. [page break ] Could your second Boy be persuaded to take a Tea cup full of it daily, It would so improve his strength & health you would not know him. docs.dcterms_abstract: In this letter, Charlotte Maitland talks of her illness and thanks Charlotte West a present she sent her. She discusses the situation in ‘that dreadful Ireland', where Charlotte West is currently residing, and the French landing there, expressing confidence that the British army will repel them effectively. She also mentions a visit of her husband ('the General') to the West household and also a letter from her son August at the front, relieved that all is well with him.

Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . Penelope Maitland to Charlotte West 10 September 1798 SOURCE: Bodleian Libraries, MS. 6633, letters, 1783–1805 Septr 10 98. My Dear Charlotte, You would have heard from me before this time, but that I have been Extreamly ill- I trust I am once more recovering my strength, which Was totally overcome, and I am oblig' d to use every means in my power Dependant on that God who alone can Bless them! The attack was the same I had suffer’d for the two months, but much more violen t & Mix’d with Bilious. Numbers here abouts have been ill, and the Strongest brought down ; what then was it to me so enfeebl'd by years, sorrows, & the former recent illness? - My Dear Charlotte , How often Do I look at your Beautiful & kind Present! I never admir’d anything So much - it Compleatly agrees with all my Ideas of the pleasing & Usefull - and now let me add my \many/ thanks for the arom: Vin:1 you were so good To send me- but I was greiv’d, my Dear, to find you had sent me a whole Bottle, and not the remains of one you had by you as yo2 Mention’d. Indeed I am greatly in your Debt, and shall rejoyce 1 Aromatic wine . 2 An abbreviation for ‘you’. Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by J. S. Ford and Charlotte Kinnear ; checked by Julian Blum ; edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . when it shall be in my power better to repay it than I have done. you are suffering, doubtless, tortures of mind as I am for the objects of our care & affection in that dreadful Ireland! the agonies of my heart from day to day, from hour to hour, keeps my strength much back - to day, news is expected - & I can never Describe what I feel under the expect ation & suspense . to add to my terrors, I dream’d a melanchol ly & very odd dream of my Dear son. God revive us by his mercy if it be his holy will! I have daily thought of you my Dr freind - well knowing your an= =xious situation . I must ever think it an extraordinary Omission In the Wise People to leave that coast unprotected, which of all Others seems to the the Easiest of access & the strongest hold for the Enemy - when Lord Cornw :3 sent back the two Regiments of Militia To England, as not wanting them , happy had it been had he sent them to Castlebar! I pray God! no more of the Enemy may land, but I don’t question but that a \much / greater force is ready – and that this Probability will [page break ] Keep the Guards there all Winter. I recd a letter from my Worthy Freind Mrs Liptrott, where -in she faithfully convey’d your Message to Totteridge. my Dear - I did not know before Capt W had had a fall from his Horse - I hope he did not receive any Hurt. It is with pleasure I tell you, the General seem’d quite Pleas’d with your visit- & I think gave a testimony of it by 3 Charles Cornwallis, first Marquess Cornwallis (1738–1805 ). In 1798 he was Lord Lieutenant of Ireland overseeing operations against the French invasion of that year. Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by J. S. Ford and Charlotte Kinnear ; checked by Julian Blum ; edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . Writing in a letter to his son Augs. “that he would present his compliments to Capt. W- informing him that We had Had the pleasure of a visit from you here, & that you were In good Health & all your children, which he imagin’d he Would be glad to hear.”- now, as it is probable, Capt W may mention this to you in a letter soon, I think it would be right, my Dear freind , for you to /improve the occasion & \ write a letter to me for the Genl. to see, expressing in that, expressing in that … Polite Language you are Mis= =tress of, your visit here, the pleasure of receiving an aquaint = =tance you had dispair’d of having again &c & particularly Noticing the General’s kind & polite attention in sending the message to capt W_- I leave these hints with you- Half hour past 2 - I have just been in the Parlor to hear a letter read from my Dr. Augs.4- it was dated from Bir5 in Tipperary - all well thank God! the attack on the French had not then taken place - but it was suppos’d the to change 8000 al= =ready with Ld. Cornw : would be sufficient to make an end of the 1500 French Devils , who he observ’d were much disap ointed of their reception in Ireland & the fewness of the people join[ing] them [page break ] nevertheless they seem to apprehend what I have said before, that 4 August, her son. 5 Birr. A place spelt ‘B ---gh’ is crossed out below . Birr is in Co. Offaly (formerly King’s County) , on the Tipperary border. Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by J. S. Ford and Charlotte Kinnear ; checked by Julian Blum ; edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at: emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . greater numbers of French are watching to get on different parts of the Irish coast. I imagin & hope you have heard from Capt. W. by this6 F[--- -]ear give my best com plts to him when you write - With those of the two Nuns, accompanied by our heartiest wishes for his happy return to England e’re long. and now Observe my Dr freind , that you are not to write the Little Letter I have mention’d on the other side, untill you have receiv’d a letter from Capt.W. mentioning the General’s message to him—- I hope yourself & sweet family continue in health ; & my dear Boy regaining strength & getting the better of all the effects of his Sad illness entirely. Remember me to your Father when you see Him - assure him he would not remember me if he was to see me. I shall ever retain the most grateful l sense of his freindship - and Very deeply Lament the Sentiments he has imbib’d So incompatible with his good understanding & discraceful to his Xtian7 Proffession - I have seen that aimable woman Mrs Garrow once since 6 There is a hole in the paper here. 7 ‘Christian’ . I hope the kind freinds who bro[ugh]t you to T_ge8, are well, and Will accept my compliments, she is the very picture of worthin ess and freindship . Sloane St. March 21st. 1799 My Dear Fr eind, How truly greiv’d am I, to have been so long silent after your two Kind letters to me! but how readily should I obtain your forgive ness , could you but know the many circumstances wch. Have occurr’d to occasion it! Believe me I receiv’d with the greatest gratitude yr kind testimony of your goodness to me in the Communicating the pleasing account from Ireland; from day to day I purpos’d to write my hearty acknowledgments, but was as often Prevented – Accept them now, my dear freind, & also for your Second Kindness to me late ly. I have had much on my mind of Va= =rious & greiving things – – Heart – depressing terrors for my son A [ugustus] : dreading his being detain’d in that most horrible Place Ireland , and for a forthnight or 3 weeks, thinking night & day he was in Imminent danger on the Sea during the Frightful storms – the hours I pass’d were truly inexpresible – Besides all this, there happen’d two or three Correspondences on most tiresom Business, the Burthe n of which wholly fell on me – I was Worried perpetuall y – and so incapable to attend to those \things/ I Most wish’d, that I have had two letters from several of my Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear and Francesco Zambonin . docs.dcterms_abstract: Penelope Maitland writes to Charlotte West to congratulate her on the birth of her child (inferred as Louisa Ann) and send her well wishes for recovery. She mentions her own son in Holland and his diarrhoea. Asks that Charlotte sends her good wishes to their friends in Sloane Square. Mentions the ongoing correspondence between their two husbands: Augustus West and Alexander Maitland.

Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Penelope Maitland to Charlotte West 20 September 1799 SOURCE: Bodleian Lib raries, MS. 6633, letters, 1783 –1805 Totteridge 20 Septr 1799 My Dear Mrs West, I yesterday had the joy of a letter from my Son1 in Holland, the date, Petten , 13th inst. but had not the same Post brought \to the Gen [era]l2/ another of a later date, viz: the 20th, the day after the last sad Engagement, I had still been under much disquietude. he was Exceedingly considerate & kind to write in so much hurry and so Fatigu'd to assure us he was well - I cannot be sufficiently thank = =full to God for his preservation now in 3 engagements! - he Had not had his Cloaths off in a Fortnight – but there is no Cessation from terror. there seems a necessity to fight every inch of the Way, exactly contrary to the first expectation - plainly it Evinces the deception the great People here were under, in fan cying the easy admittance into Holland. Augustus commission' d me To tell you, my dear Fre ind, Capt West3 was perfectly well, and not \to all appearance/ 1 Augustus, s on of Penelope Maitland, fighting in the Netherlands . According to Burke’s Peerage , he was mortally wounded at Egmont on Zec [sic], 6 Oct 1797. This error is repeated subsequently, e .g. in ‘thepeerage.com’. The battle was Egmond - aan-Zee (or the Battle of Alkmaar), and took place 2 Oct 1799 - see https://en.w ikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Alkmaar_(1799) . If Augustus was wounded on 6 October, it was more likely to have been in the final battle of the campaign, the Battle of Castricum – see https://e n.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Castricum . 2 The ‘General’ refers to Alexander Maitland, husband of the writer . 3 Captain Charles Augustus West, husband of Charlotte West . Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 in any \respect/ the worse for all he had undergone . in my answer, which Went yesterday, I with much pleasure sent the good account I had Had of & from you. I wish I could attain to some measure of your Laudable Fortitude in not anticipating evil. much depends I beli eve on People's natural Temper – some happily Born with a disposition to a chearful hope, & others to sad appre = =hension. now the latter, I Inherit from my Father, and my good sister was blest w ith the former from my mother. – what I \lately/ Endur'd after the Second engagement under 3 day's suspense abt. My son, can never be express'd. when God graciously releiv'd me by a Line from my son Frederick in London, whose letter on opening my eyes first met with the following words, [page break ] ‘Augustus is quite well & untouch'd - I have just receiv'd a lettr ‘from Sr Ralp [h] Aber cromby’4 may the divine goodness be Continu'd to us, my dear fre ind to the happy restoration of those who now occupy our anxious thoughts! the General desires his best compliments as do P . & C.5 and We all unite in being truly glad your Late & Long sufferings With little Louisa -Ann,6 have been so amply repaid. I am in debt for Sloane Square7, but shall with pleasure Discharge it w [he]n. I have opport [uni]ty. at present I am full of wri = 4 Lieutenant -General Sir Ralph Abercromb y, Commander -in-Chief of the British Troops in the Netherlands . 5 Penelope and Cha rlotte, daughters of the writer . 6 Louisa -Ann, sixth child of Charlotte West, born 7 July 1799 , who died young . 7 Penelope Maitland stayed at 5 Sloane Street in March 1799 . I shall ever esteem a Letter from you a great pleasure my Dear Mrs. West – May I ask after your father8, how does he Do? – the Loss you regret in this neighbourhood, is re = =gretted by all – I do not know whether I may not include the Widower of the aimable Mrs. Garrow9 – for he is almost Invisible , and not only in never coming to see any body, But by signifying his wish & Intention that no body shall see him – Being about to Build a Wall 12 feet high in Front of his House! shutting out the Be autiful l Prospect Which is so valuable a circumstance to it. the reason he gave lately to a Neighbour who happen'd to meet him, was, ‘He was Sick of the World & neither desir'd to see, or hear ‘of it, mor e-’he now & then appears at church however and is ve ry Polite & Freindly to me w[he]n. I accost him. he has [page break ] Painted his House white which is thought by some to give It an elegance. this white washing distemper has ran thro' all the Village with very few exceptions – Mr. Manning's Is the most improv'd by it I ever saw. 8 Sampson Perry, father of Charlotte West . 9 Mrs Garrow died in 1798, according to an obituary in The European Magazine and London Review . Turing10 are well. [Address] Mrs. Charles West Hans Place Brompton Knightsbridge 28 Septr. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 Penelope Maitland to Charlotte West 5 February 1800 SOURCE: Bodleian Lib raries, MS. 6633, letters, 1783 –1805 Totteridge 5th Feb: 1800 My Dear Freind, your kind attention to me, your sympathetick feelings for me1, and your enquiries after me, particularly by your truly fre indly Letter of Decr.2d will ever have a place in my most gratefull Remembrance – accept my Sincere , tho’ shamefully delay’d acknow -ledgments & thanks from my own hand ; my Dear Mrs. Liptrott Has I know kindly transmitted them according to my request, and I doubt not your kindness in accepting them thr ’o her from my heart - All language would fail, oh my Dear Freind! should I attempt To Describe my sorrows or Calcula te my Loss – the world can Never repair it to me – and the dark cloud must rest [ -word struck through -] Immoveable upon all my few days of Earthly Pilgrimage – May I have grace so to improve the divine dispensations, that In the end I may find cause to sa y with Holy David, ‘ it Is good fo r me that I have been afflicted’ – my Path has \long/ been Thick strown with sorrow & greif, but this calamity out-weighs 1 Penelope Maitland’s son, Col onel Augustus Maitland, had been killed in the Netherlands in October 1799, during the Anglo -Russian expedition. See the letters in this correspondence of 1799. Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear and Phoebe Bradley ; checked by Amy Holguin ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 All – nor can any time soften its severity to my inward Feelings, whatever outward appearance I impose on myself for the sake of my Freinds. – there were some anecdotes I Inserted in my Letter to Mrs Liptrott, which probably you heard, & therefore forbear repeating them – one was the Chapter I heard Read in this Church the last Sunday my dr son & his B[rothe]r. Fred [eric]k: Were here at church with me – the other, some Lines wch forcd Themselves upon me one morng. Early while I was dressing my Head, which were in a style of strong Presentiment – another was my [page break ] extraordinary & melancholly Dream just after the fatal wound before the new of it had reach’d me , which has added to the many Instances that have confrim’d my Faith in Dreams forever – I will, when time permits, send you some other Lines the Produce of an afflicted Heart, written un der the various Impulses of sorrow, Hope, Fear, and the Last dreadful catastrophe, which put an End to Hope & Seal’d the Irreversible doom of Greif . – oh my Dear Freind! what daily pangs do I suffer when I behold the Lov’d little Room he us’d to inhabit here, and the many Pritty kind gifts of Pictures, shells &c &c in my \own/ room with Which he adorn’d it! – my eyes ever bend towards them, tho’ my Heart is agoniz’d by them – oh that the Eyes of \my/ Faith Were open’d to look up to that blessed state wher e Tears shall be W ip’d away from all Faces! May we meet in Jesu’s arms, Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear and Phoebe Bradley ; checked by Amy Holguin ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 3 free’d from trouble & all harms, Near thy throne for ever wait, Bless thee for Ea rth’s painful state; Pilgrimage for ever past, Joys that shall for ever last! Amidst my Sorrows, beleive me, my dear Freind, truly rejoic’d for that great Providential Mercy which terminated your Anxious fears, & restor’d to you a Belov’d Husband and the Father of your little Family – I beg both yourself & Him to accept My Sincere congra tulations, wi th my earnest wishes for your Continu’d Happiness together, & that he may not be further [page break ] Involv’d in this dreadfull, necessary War, to which nothing but Infinite Wisdom & a llmighty Power, can put a happy end! The affairs in Ireland I think threaten us with the greatest terrors, and that a Union , if accomplish’d, will be bought too dear . the ignorance, Bigotry & savageness of that People, are dreadfull things to contend with! I really think, the situation of Coll: Cunningham of the Guar \ds/ from his Wound, transcends all I ever heard, & that the Sight of any near & dear to one, in such a state of ceaseless & Irremediable suffering, is worse than Even their death. I am lately inform’d that he, having no mouth, Jaws or tongue , is fed only at the top of his Windpipe!! pray my dear Does Cap t West ever visit him, & what his account of Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear and Phoebe Bradley ; checked by Amy Holguin ; checked and edited by Mike Webb. I hope the Paragraph in the Papers of his intended marriage is quite unfounded . I read the Death of a Mrs. Turing, Sloane Street, I should be glad to hear it was not your particular & agreable Freind, Mrs John Turing?2 – Mr. Ed: Garrow’s3 little Son, has been dangerously ill many Days, Hooping cough, violent fever &c – he is thought better, but far from recover’d – Mr Garrow is ill himself these last two days – much illness has been about, every where dreadfull Fevers attended by such Pains in the side as, as have requir’d Bleeding as likely to kill as to Cure. Mrs Dury of Hadley, had a Pound taken from her for 3 days successiv ely & young Mr Neate 16 ozs. one day – [page break ] It is amazing the Faculty have found out no easier remedy than this which is so distructive to the Nerves & health In other respects. W. Can gratifye it, I shall Ever be gratefull – it is to have a representation of the Mournfull Spot where he was Consign’d to Earth – if ever So rude & imperfect a sketch – – what ever object of Trees or house &c made it remarkable.
